clue.text: Monstrously stab king, and profit? It's hard to fathom

indicators.note: done monstrously, the letters of stab are mangled into a new order

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for king (Latin rex)
to profit by something is to use it

explanation.surface: A Macbeth-like plot to stab a king and gain from it, which seems beyond understanding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Monstrously' is the anagram signal on stab alone; king and profit then follow as plain synonyms in clue order.
explanation.definitionFit: Something abstruse is obscure and difficult to understand, hence hard to fathom.

clue.text: Exclamation from Scot pierced by end of skean-dhu that hurts!

indicators.note: something pierced has another thing driven into it, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: och is a Scottish exclamation of surprise or regret

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: A Highlander stabbed with his own dagger cries out in pain.
explanation.walkthrough: A skean-dhu is the small dagger tucked into a Highland kilt stocking; its last letter U goes inside OCH.
explanation.definitionFit: An interjection of sudden pain, the cry someone gives when something hurts.

clue.text: Accursed like dog dismissed in dramatic scene?

definitions.text: like dog dismissed in dramatic scene?
definitions.meaning: Lady Macbeth cries 'Out; Spot is a typical dog's name, so the spot dismissed is a cursed dog

explanation.surface: A cursed creature, like a dog sent packing in a stage scene.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading takes Lady Macbeth's 'spot' (a bloodstain) as a dog called Spot.
explanation.definitionFit: Condemned or cursed things are described with this word, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Wife with some scores not easy to bear

parts.note: a score is twenty, so four scores make eighty

explanation.surface: A wife who keeps a tally of grievances becomes hard to put up with.
explanation.definitionFit: A heavy load is difficult to carry, and figuratively serious matters are hard to bear.

clue.text: Author is hard to follow, like others of his ilk

parts.note: Sir Walter Scott, the novelist
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A writer whose prose is hard going, much like the rest of his kind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to follow' just says H comes last. 'His ilk' points back to the author: Walter Scott and his countrymen were Scots.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Walter Scott came from Edinburgh, so others of his kind share his nationality, from Scotland.

clue.text: Mac, in short, butchered for kingship

indicators.note: letters that are butchered are hacked about into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Macbeth, named in short as Mac, killed a king to seize the crown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'butchered' rearranges all ten letters of MAC IN SHORT.
explanation.definitionFit: A supporter of royal rule favours government by a king, so is for kingship.

clue.text: Interrupt speech with diabolical cheek about line

indicators.note: about means around, so the anagram goes round the other letter
diabolical means fiendishly bad, so the word cheek is wrecked into a new order

explanation.surface: A speaker is cut short by someone with devilish impudence about a single line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'diabolical' makes HECKE from CHEEK; 'about' puts it around L.
explanation.definitionFit: To break in on a speaker with jeers or awkward questions is to barrack them.

clue.text: Convert a doubter not easily swayed

indicators.note: to convert something is to change it into another form, so these letters are reshaped

explanation.surface: Trying to win over a sceptic who will not be moved.
explanation.definitionFit: Stubborn and unyielding people refuse to change their minds.

clue.text: Hag's warning of stormy period once engulfing monarch

indicators.note: engulfing means swallowing up, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: a storm cone was a canvas cone hoisted at British coastal stations to warn of gales, now discontinued
R is the abbreviation for a monarch (rex or regina)

explanation.surface: One of Macbeth's witches warns of coming storms that will swallow a king.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words name an ugly or malicious old woman, especially a witch.

clue.text: State of role you reportedly rejected

indicators.note: rejected means turned back, so the pieces are read in the other direction

parts.note: a hat is a role, as in wearing two hats

indicators.note: reportedly means as heard, so the word you is given by its sound

parts.note: the letter U sounds like you

explanation.surface: Turning down a part an actor was offered.
explanation.definitionFit: A US state, the one whose capital is Salt Lake City.

clue.text: Close discussions about wife showing nocturnal activity

definitions.note: singular phrase for a plural noun naming such outings

parts.note: nigh means near or close

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one word goes around the other

parts.note: talks are discussions

explanation.surface: Private negotiations concerning a wife reveal what goes on after dark.
explanation.walkthrough: Lady Macbeth's sleepwalking is the theme's nocturnal activity.
explanation.definitionFit: Walks taken after dark, such as sleepwalking, are things done at night.

clue.text: Referred to toil and trouble, say, sorted out in proof, finally

definitions.text: Referred to toil and trouble, say

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so the jumble goes within the other piece

parts.note: QED (quod erat demonstrandum) is written at the end of a mathematical proof

indicators.note: sorted means put in order differently, so the word out is rearranged

explanation.surface: Talk of the witches' toil and trouble, sorted out in the final proof.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sorted' turns OUT into UOT, placed 'in' QED. 'Toil and trouble' is the witches' refrain from Macbeth.
explanation.definitionFit: Repeating someone's words, such as the witches' chant, is citing them.

clue.text: The average grade in a test for stage

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so the grade sits within the other piece

parts.note: a trial is a test
C is a middling mark in exams

explanation.surface: A mediocre mark in an exam, perhaps for drama school.
explanation.definitionFit: Anything belonging to drama or the performing world is for the stage.

clue.text: For one looking for birdies, a bad putter?

definitions.meaning: a keen birdwatcher who chases rare sightings
a golfer whose hands jerk nervously on the green, a sufferer from the yips

explanation.surface: A golfer chasing birdies (one under par) but undone on the green.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For' is a link word; the golf picture hides the birdwatching sense.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang names an obsessive birdwatcher this way, and a jittery golfer twitches over putts.

clue.text: Divine female that hero meets at end of the 5 24 across

definitions.text: that hero meets at end of the 5 24 across
definitions.meaning: the hero of the Scottish play, Macbeth, meets his downfall in Macduff at its end

explanation.surface: A goddess whom the play's protagonist encounters at the close.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Scottish play' is the theatre's superstitious name for Macbeth.
explanation.definitionFit: A goddess of vengeance, and in general use one's inescapable agent of downfall.

clue.text: Actions of insignificant taleteller?

parts.note: Macbeth calls life 'a tale told by an idiot, signifying nothing', so the teller of that insignificant tale is a fool, and a fool's acts are follies

explanation.surface: What a trivial storyteller gets up to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Insignificant' means literally 'signifying nothing', echoing the Tomorrow speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Foolish acts are what a fool does, like the idiot in the famous speech.

clue.text: Triumphantly elevated, presided over country riven by outrage

indicators.note: riven means split apart, so the country is split open with the other piece inside

parts.note: Chad is a country in Africa
ire is anger, outrage

explanation.surface: A leader carried shoulder-high in a nation torn by anger.
explanation.walkthrough: Two senses share the one word: carried aloft on a chair in triumph, and presided over a meeting.
explanation.definitionFit: Carried shoulder-high by a crowd in celebration, and also ran a meeting as its head.

clue.text: Established a title that's raised issues

indicators.note: in a down clue raised means read upwards, so the pieces run backwards

parts.note: to set something is to establish it
a name is a title

explanation.surface: A newly founded title brings up fresh problems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' turns SETANAME upwards in this down light.
explanation.definitionFit: To issue forth is to flow out from a source, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Returns in a tragedy's leading part — touching

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so one piece goes within the other
the leading part of a word is its first letter

parts.note: returns on an investment are gains

explanation.surface: Profits in the lead role of a tragedy, a moving thing.
explanation.definitionFit: Leaning against a wall means in contact with it, so touching it.

clue.text: Helping in crime, a risky activity

parts.note: betting is gambling, a risky pastime

explanation.surface: Assisting a criminal is a dangerous game.
explanation.definitionFit: The legal phrase aiding and abetting means assisting someone to commit an offence.

clue.text: Inspiring act the Bard unceasingly revised

indicators.note: revised means altered and reworked, so the letters are reordered
without ceasing, that is with no end, so the final letter goes

explanation.surface: Shakespeare kept reworking an uplifting scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unceasingly' cuts BARD to BAR; 'revised' shuffles THE + BAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Inspiration literally means drawing air into the lungs, so inhaling is the act.

clue.text: Bard having cast first murderer

indicators.note: to cast off one's first is to shed the opening letter, so the leading letter of the poet's name goes

parts.note: Walt Whitman, the American poet, called the Bard of Democracy

explanation.surface: Shakespeare casting the First Murderer, one of the hired killers in Macbeth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bard' wants to be Shakespeare; here it is Walt Whitman, who 'having cast first' loses his W. First Murderer is a part in Macbeth.
explanation.definitionFit: A hired killer, the contract assassin of crime fiction, is a kind of murderer.

clue.text: Among makers of awful gruel, American serving regional dish

indicators.note: among means placed amid others, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: Macbeth's witches, or hags, brew a gruesome potion thickened 'thick and slab' like gruel
a GI is a serving American soldier

explanation.surface: An American soldier eating among bad cooks gets a local speciality.
explanation.walkthrough: Haggis is Scotland's national pudding of offal, oats and suet.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scottish speciality associated with one region, eaten on Burns Night.

clue.text: Grumbling about couple holding hands that's delightful

indicators.note: about means around, so one word surrounds the other

parts.note: bitching is slang for complaining
in bridge East and West are partners, a pair holding hands of cards

explanation.surface: Complaining about a pair of lovebirds who hold hands.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'hands' are bridge hands, not romantic ones.
explanation.definitionFit: Charming in a magical way, enchanting, so delightful.

clue.text: Having set out after power, act

indicators.note: after says the second piece comes later than the first in the answer

parts.note: to lay something is to set it out, as a table

explanation.surface: Having set off, one moves only after gaining power.
explanation.definitionFit: To perform, as an actor does on stage, is to take part in a drama.

clue.text: Caledonian featured in epic tale

indicators.note: featured in means appearing inside, so the letters lie within these words

explanation.surface: A Scot who appears in a heroic story.
explanation.definitionFit: Caledonia was the Roman name for Scotland, whose ancient people were Picts.

clue.text: Article about second chief of clan

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: the definite article
a second article, the indefinite one

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece about the deputy leader of a Highland family.
explanation.walkthrough: Macbeth was Thane of Glamis and of Cawdor; a thane was a Scottish clan chief or lord.
explanation.definitionFit: In medieval Scotland a lord holding land from the king, often heading a clan.

clue.text: Beat with cane and made a change

definitions.meaning: struck with a thin flexible rod

explanation.surface: A punishment followed by a change of heart.
explanation.definitionFit: A switch is a thin cane used to whip, and to switch is also to exchange.
